title: Start here
subtitle: What this manual covers and how to use it

blocks.text: This is a practical guide to StepCAS, the nps application presented through Ki V4 on the TI-Nspire CX II. It starts with the keys and follows the ordinary tasks of entering mathematics, reading explanations and saving work. You do not need to know Lua, C++ or how the calculator was built.

Read Your first session if the app is already installed. Use Opening StepCAS if you are at the Home screen. The command reference near the end is for looking things up after you have tried the tutorials.

Our application and its mathematical walkthrough engine.
The document that displays the entry line, history and walkthroughs.
The algebra engine used for ordinary calculations and some checks.
The runtime that allows the native module to run.

blocks.title: Edition and evidence
blocks.text: Prepared 9 September 2026 from the current working source. This is an unreleased development build, not a promise that every feature is on your installed package. The pictures use retained emulator captures and TI product photographs. Annotated plates are teaching illustrations. They are not new photos of your handheld or proof of a fresh device test.

Expected answers in the lessons are mathematical targets. Equivalent algebraic forms are acceptable. A screenshot can show older wording while the nearby instructions describe the current source. The manual covers everyday calculator use and the current StepCAS interface. Advanced TI applications and the much larger Giac command library have their own linked references.

title: Your first session
subtitle: Get one result, open its explanation and return to the entry line

items: Turn on the calculator with Home / On. Choose Browse under Documents and open the installed StepCAS document, usually named nps_v4.
Wait for the application to finish loading. A Giac OK message identifies the algebra engine. Read any dependency or integrity error before proceeding.
Select the entry box at the bottom. Type !s 2*x+3=11 and press Enter. The exclamation mark is available from the punctuation palette.
Look for the answer x = 4. In the step list, use Up and Down to select a step. Press Enter to open its explanation.
Press Shift+Tab to switch between Standard and Beginner detail. Beginner gives more explanation. It does not change the answer.
Press Escape once to return to the list and again to return to the entry screen. Save the document with Ctrl+S.

blocks.title: What you should understand
blocks.text: Subtracting 3 from both sides gives 2*x = 8. Dividing both sides by 2 gives x = 4. Substituting 4 into the original left side gives 11.

title: Meet the calculator
subtitle: Find the physical controls before learning shortcuts

blocks.name: keypad
blocks.caption: Annotated TI product photo. The white calculator is the CX II. The darker model behind it is a CAS model. Their built-in symbolic capabilities differ.

blocks.text: Press the outer edges of the touchpad for Up, Down, Left and Right. Sliding a finger moves the pointer. The center click selects an item. For a first lesson, the directional edges and Enter are easier to control than pointer movement.

Ctrl is blue. Hold it while pressing another key to use that key’s blue function. Shift changes the next character or activates a shifted shortcut. A shortcut written Ctrl+S means hold Ctrl, press S, then release.

blocks.title: You are using two layers
blocks.text: Home and Doc belong to the calculator system. StepCAS supplies its own entry screen, menu and walkthrough controls. A key can do different things in those places. The screen’s footer is the best immediate reminder.
Source: TI Handheld Keys and Keyboard Shortcuts [T1, T2].

blocks.text: In step details, Escape returns to the list. From the step list it returns to the entry screen. Use Home to reach the calculator Home screen. Do not use Ctrl+Escape as a universal “back” shortcut. Its behavior is context dependent.

For punctuation such as !, quotes and a colon, open the punctuation palette. For square brackets, use the blue bracket function with Ctrl and the parenthesis key. Move the cursor out of a fraction or exponent before typing the next argument.
Sources: [T1, T2] and current StepCAS event handling.

subtitle: Start from Home and choose the document

title: The entry screen and its menu
subtitle: Where commands go and how results are kept

blocks.name: tool-palette-boxes.png
blocks.caption: Retained emulator screenshot of the StepCAS palette. The down marker means more categories are below the visible list.

blocks.text: The bottom box is the editable entry line. Earlier inputs and outputs occupy the history above it. The title nps_v4 identifies the document. The top system bar can show page numbers, angle mode and battery status.

items: Return to the entry screen with Escape before inserting a new command from a menu.
Press Menu. Use Up and Down to select a category and Enter to open it. Use Escape to back out.
Choose the command by its name. Many entries insert only the beginning of a call, such as diff(. Complete the expression, variable and closing parenthesis.
Review the input box before pressing Enter. A menu label describes the arguments but is not always a complete runnable example.

blocks.title: The menu you see matters
blocks.text: TI’s built-in Calculator menu is different from the StepCAS menu. StepCAS includes Physics, Templates and Steps. The separate native KhiCAS shell can have another menu layout.

Templates insert a starting structure for a fraction, power, root, derivative, integral or equation. A template helps you type. It does not guarantee that a native walkthrough exists for the resulting problem.

title: Typing mathematics correctly
subtitle: Use grouping and explicit arguments

rows: Use * when you want to avoid ambiguous adjacency.
Group the entire numerator and denominator.
Use Right to leave the superscript slot.
A function has parentheses around its argument.
The comma separates the expression and variable.
= states equality. It does not store a value.
Square brackets contain the list elements.
Each inner list is one row.
Two dots separate the lower and upper bounds.

blocks.text: The examples show the intended expression, not a promise that each printed character corresponds to a separate keypress. The native editor turns powers and fractions into two-dimensional slots. Look at the cursor before typing a comma, plus sign or closing parenthesis.

blocks.title: A useful input check
blocks.text: Before Enter, count the arguments and check the grouping. For diff((x+1)/(x-2),x), the first comma comes after the whole fraction. If it is still in an exponent or denominator slot, use the arrow keys to leave that slot.

Use the negative-number key for a leading negative if the editor distinguishes it from subtraction. Use plain x for the variable rather than the multiplication symbol. Letter case can matter for stored names.

title: History, copying and clearing
subtitle: Reuse work without accidentally deleting it

blocks.text: History contains inputs and displayed outputs. Use Tab and the arrow keys to move focus from the entry line into history. The focused editor or highlighted entry tells you which item will receive an action.

items: Select the old input or output you want to reuse.
Press Enter to copy it into the entry line. This gives you an opportunity to edit before evaluating again.
Change the numbers or expression, then press Enter from the entry line to calculate.
For more control on a focused history item, open its context menu and choose Copy to Entry Line or Delete Entry.

rows: Removes the character before the cursor.
Asks for confirmation before clearing all history. The current unentered input is preserved.
Resets the algebra session. This is separate from clearing visible history.

blocks.title: Focus first
blocks.text: Ctrl+Del is not harmless everywhere. In history it is an entry-deletion action. Check that the cursor is in the bottom input field before using it to clear a line.

History is not an archive of all derivation trees. The last retained walkthrough can be reopened with !! during the session. Saving and reopening the document preserves history text, but a walkthrough must be computed again.

title: Read a walkthrough
subtitle: Follow the answer, the evidence and the individual steps

blocks.name: results
blocks.caption: Annotated retained captures. These show older heading wording. Current builds can show more explicit result classifications and detail labels.

rows: The problem that was submitted. A shortened preview may omit its end.
The result, if one is available and hints permit it to be shown.
Whether a check ran, whether it agreed and whether work is complete.
Conditions under which the mathematics or physical model applies.
The physical interpretation, when the solver supplies one.
The plan, transformations, checks and cases that make up the explanation.

blocks.text: Select a step and press Enter. Current transformation details use Do for the operation, Write for the resulting expression and Why for its justification. They also retain the starting expression and conditions. Plans and checks show different information because they are different kinds of records.

blocks.title: Read the status before copying
blocks.text: An answer supplied by Giac can coexist with some native steps. A visible value does not mean StepCAS produced a complete verified explanation of that value.

title: Move through the steps
subtitle: Select, expand and open the explanation you need

blocks.name: walkthrough
blocks.caption: Annotated older emulator captures. The integral shown assumes x > 0. The plus and minus markers identify a folded or expanded group.

rows: Up/Down selects steps. Left folds a group. Right expands it. On a row without children, Left/Right moves between steps.
Up/Down scrolls its explanation. Left/Right moves to another visible step.
Enter or Escape returns to the list.
Escape returns to the entry screen.
Click once to select a row. Click the selected row again to open it.

blocks.text: A group contains smaller steps. Folding it reduces clutter without deleting any mathematics. This is especially helpful for the product rule, quotient rule or a physics solution that contains an algebra calculation.

blocks.title: Nothing is recalculated when browsing
blocks.text: Opening a detail page, folding a branch or changing the explanation level reads the existing result. If you want to solve a changed problem, return to the entry screen and submit the new input.

title: Beginner detail and hint mode
subtitle: Control how much explanation you see

blocks.text: Beginner detail and hint progression are separate settings. Beginner detail makes explanations fuller. Hint progression controls when the next part of the work and the final answer become visible.

items: For fuller explanations, open a walkthrough and press Shift+Tab. Check the header for BEGINNER. Press it again to return to STANDARD.
For hints, return to the entry screen and enter !h on. You can also choose Steps > Hint walkthrough (Tab next).
Submit a supported problem, such as !s 2*x+3=11. Try the next operation on paper before pressing Tab.
Press Tab to reveal more work. Repeat until the walkthrough is fully exposed.
To return to full walkthroughs for subsequent requests, enter !h off or choose Steps > Full walkthrough (all steps).

blocks.title: Hints are not an answer checker
blocks.text: You do not enter your proposed next line into the walkthrough. It reveals recorded work. A parent step’s completed expression can stay hidden until its child work has been revealed.

blocks.title: Commands without native steps behave differently
blocks.text: A Giac answer with no walkthrough can appear immediately. Hint mode cannot create missing steps or turn a limits command into a limit lesson.
If TAB result is displayed after the answer becomes available, Tab may open the complete result instead of advancing hints. Follow the footer and return to the list with Escape.

title: Read long expressions and explanations
subtitle: Use the complete text when a preview is too small

blocks.text: A calculator screen has limited space. A shortened input, crowded formula or trailing dots mean you may be looking at a preview. Do not copy an incomplete denominator, unit or condition from it.

rows: Press T, or use Actions > Read Full Text.
Use Actions > Read Full Text. The Help action also opens the reader.
Press Tab to open the complete answer view when hint progression permits it.

items: Open the full-text reader. Use Up and Down to scroll one line at a time.
Use Tab to move forward by a larger amount. Shift+Tab moves back.
Press Escape or Enter to close the reader and return to the originating view.

blocks.text: Full Text favors readable, wrapped text over two-dimensional notation. It retains the whole expression. The answer view and step details can still use native math boxes when the expression fits.

blocks.title: Help has a special meaning inside a walkthrough
blocks.text: There, Help changes Standard/Beginner detail. Use T when you specifically want Full Text. The reader respects hint withholding and does not reveal future steps.

Actions > Increase Font Size and Decrease Font Size adjust the shell/history font. The walkthrough has its own fitting rules. If increasing the font makes a history expression too large, use the full reader rather than assuming the expression was lost.

title: Automatic commands and explicit modes
subtitle: Know what the next press of Enter will do

blocks.text: A fresh document starts with automatic walkthrough recognition. Commands such as solve(...), diff(...) and int(...) are checked for a native explanation. Other ordinary expressions go to Giac. Saved preferences can change this starting behavior.

rows: Differentiate this expression once using the selected variable.
!k find v, v0=5 m/s, a=3 m/s^2, t=4 s
Solve this structured kinematics problem once.
Select differentiation as the persistent mode for following input.
Select integration, solving or kinematics in the same way.
Use t as the selected variable for prefix commands.
Clear the selected solver mode and switch to plain Giac.
Reopen the most recent retained walkthrough.

blocks.title: Return to ordinary automatic operation
blocks.text: Enter !g on its own line. Then enter !h off on another line. The first clears a persistent solver mode. The second re-enables automatic recognition with full walkthroughs.

!g
!h off
!v x

The commands above are separate submissions. !g is a mode switch, not a prefix that evaluates text after it. In a persistent !d mode, type x^3 rather than diff(x^3,x), because the whole following input is treated as the expression to differentiate.

title: Arithmetic, fractions and decimal answers
subtitle: Understand the number before changing its appearance

rows: 14, because multiplication is performed before addition.
A decimal approximation to one third.
An exact radical in Giac when exact evaluation is active.

blocks.text: An exact answer represents the value without rounding. A decimal is often more convenient for measurement or plotting, but the final digits can be rounded. A fraction and its decimal approximation are not different solutions.

Use Number > Convert to Decimal or type evalf(...). Complete the argument and closing parenthesis. For teaching steps, start with integer values and exact fractions so you stay inside the widest supported walkthrough coverage.

blocks.title: There are separate numeric settings
blocks.text: TI document settings, Giac settings and the native StepCAS numeric mode are not one shared switch. The current Ki V4 walkthrough calls use the native default Exact mode. A TI status-bar setting does not establish that a native request used Decimal mode.

Physics precision is another distinction. A supplied measured value can carry significant figures even while the internal arithmetic uses exact fractions. Keep the units and the original decimal places when entering a measurement.

title: Solve equations
subtitle: Find the unknown and check it in the original equation

items: Return to ordinary automatic operation, or use the explicit !s prefix.
Enter solve(2*x+3=11,x). Read the answer and open the steps.
Check that the explanation subtracts 3 and divides by 2.
Substitute the answer into the original equation yourself: 2*4+3 = 11.

rows: No solution. Cancelling x leaves an impossible equality.
Every value is a solution within the stated domain.
The pure-square family can return x = -3 and x = 3.

blocks.title: Current native coverage
blocks.text: Linear equations in one unknown are supported. The separate quadratic family handles pure squares with exact rational roots, such as x^2=9. It does not establish a general quadratic-formula walkthrough for x^2+x-1=0 or a radical-root walkthrough for x^2=2.

Giac can solve more forms than the native teaching engine. When the app supplies a CAS answer, read that label. For an equation outside the teaching coverage, you can deliberately switch to !g and run solve(...), but the result is then ordinary CAS output.

title: Rearrange, simplify, expand and factor
subtitle: Choose the operation that matches your goal

rows: I = V/R, with R not zero.

blocks.text: Simplifying changes the form of an expression. Solving finds values that make an equation true. Factoring is useful for seeing products and zeros, but factor(...) by itself does not ask for an equation’s solution set.

items: Choose Algebra > Simplify, Expand or Factor. Complete the call and press Enter.
Open a transformation and read Do, Write and Why.
For a factorization, multiply the result back out to check that it matches the original expression.

blocks.title: Where the native explanation stops
blocks.text: Formula rearrangement supports a single occurrence of the target symbol through supported inverse operations. Polynomial rewrite steps cover exact arithmetic, common factors and supported monic quadratic factoring. General rational simplification, decimal inputs, radicals and higher-degree factoring can exceed that coverage.

An expression already in the requested form can finish without a transformation. This is a valid outcome. Extra steps should not be invented just to make the list longer. Read any conditions introduced by division or reciprocals.

title: Differentiate a function
subtitle: Find a rate of change with named rules

blocks.text:
diff(x^3,x)
!d sin(x)
diff((x+1)/(x-2),x)

items: Use Calculus > Derivative or type diff(x^3,x). The first argument is the function. The second is the variable.
For x^3, expect 3*x^2. Open the power-rule step to see how the exponent is used.
Try a product or quotient and expand its group. The smaller steps calculate the derivatives needed by the main rule.
Read any domain restrictions. A denominator must remain nonzero where the formula is used.

blocks.title: Which rules have native steps
blocks.text: The implementation covers constants, the variable, sums, constant multiples, products, quotients, integer powers, the chain rule and supported sin, cos, tan, exp, ln and sqrt forms. Particular domains and input shapes can still cause a refusal.

Implicit differentiation, partial-derivative lessons and higher derivatives in a single request are outside the native walkthrough family. A different letter works when explicitly supplied, for example diff(t^3,t). For prefix entry, select it with !v t and restore !v x when finished.

blocks.title: About the input appearance
blocks.text: The current input may show diff(...) as a function call. A stacked editable d/dx template is not established as working in this build. The textbook-style input discussed earlier has not been implemented by this manual.

title: Integrate a function
subtitle: Find an antiderivative and remember the constant

blocks.text:
int(x^2,x)
int(sin(x),x)
int(exp(2*x),x)

rows: ln(x) + C on the stated x > 0 branch

blocks.text: An indefinite integral describes a family of functions. C is the constant of integration. Differentiating C gives zero, so every value of that constant has the same derivative.

items: Choose Calculus > Integral and complete int(x^2,x).
Read the antiderivative and open the rule steps. The native integrator checks its answer by differentiating it.
For a linear argument such as exp(2*x), look for the substitution or scale correction.
Read the assumptions for reciprocal and logarithmic cases before using the answer.

blocks.title: Do not silently discard a domain condition
blocks.text: The positive branch ln(x) is not a claim about negative x. The general real antiderivative of 1/x on intervals avoiding zero is ln(abs(x)) + C. Use the branch and conditions actually reported by StepCAS.

blocks.title: Current native limits
blocks.text: The supported lessons include sums, constant multiples, integer powers, reciprocals and sin, cos or exp with supported linear arguments. Integration by parts, nonlinear substitution and general integrals involving tan, ln, sqrt or rational exponents are outside this family.

For a definite integral such as int(x^2,x,0,1), the expected value is 1/3. Definite-integral walkthroughs are not supported. Use ordinary Giac deliberately when you need the calculation and read the result as CAS output.

title: Limits, sums and products
subtitle: Use Giac for the value and recognize the absence of native lessons

items: Enter !g on its own line to select ordinary Giac.
Enter a complete limit, sum or product expression from the examples below.
Check the approach value, index and bounds carefully.
When finished, enter !h off to restore automatic full walkthrough recognition.

rows: Approach zero from both sides, in radians.
Approach the removable hole at x=1.

blocks.text: A limit asks what values are approached. It does not necessarily ask for the value at the point itself. In the second example, the original fraction is undefined at x=1 even though the limit exists.

blocks.title: Native limit walkthroughs are not implemented
blocks.text: The Calculus menu exposes limit(...) through Giac. It does not provide a limit-rule derivation, a continuity lesson or L’Hopital steps. The sum and product examples here are also ordinary CAS calculations.

Use the word infinity for an infinite bound in Giac syntax. An unevaluated expression is not a proof that a limit or sum does not exist. Check the command, domain and backend response. Source for Giac limit direction and sequence syntax: [G1, G2].

title: Guided physics
subtitle: Start with a supplied problem before entering your own model

blocks.name: physics
blocks.caption: Annotated retained emulator captures of the Physics menu and guided browser. Current labels are matched against the source.

items: Return to the entry screen. Choose Menu > Physics > Guided physics problems.
Use Up and Down to select an example. Read the description at the bottom. Press T if it is shortened.
Press Enter to run the selected example. It opens the usual walkthrough viewer.
Use Escape to return to the entry screen. Reopen the Physics browser from its menu when you want another example.

blocks.title: These are supplied examples
blocks.text: The browser is not a general editable physics worksheet. Its stored examples cover unit conversion, density, kinematics, vectors, work, components, an incompatible-unit refusal, catch-up and relative motion. The selected example runs with its prepared quantities.

For your own one-dimensional kinematics numbers, use the Physics menu templates or !k input described next. Other structured solver capabilities exist in the native interface but do not all have general input forms in the current document.

title: Enter your own motion problem
subtitle: Use constant acceleration along one axis

blocks.text: !k find v, v0 = 5 m/s, a = 3 m/s^2, t = 4 s

rows: Initial velocity at the start of the interval

items: Decide which direction is positive. Write the unknown after find.
Enter the known quantities with units. Separate quantities with commas or the supported semicolon syntax.
Press Enter. Read the assumptions and the chosen equation.
For the example, the model uses v = v0 + a*t. Substitution gives 5 + 3*4 = 17 m/s.

blocks.title: The menu says speed and distance in places
blocks.text: The signed one-axis model uses velocity and displacement. A negative result can mean motion in the negative direction. If an object reverses direction, total distance traveled and signed displacement are different quantities.
Try changing only v0 to 18 km/h. That is 5 m/s, so the same acceleration and time still give 17 m/s. The conversion should be part of the explanation.

The planner can use an intermediate quantity when one equation is not enough. It still has a limited collection of constant-acceleration equations and algebra routes. Missing information, an unsupported square-root step or an incompatible unit can stop it. The !k entry is not a solver for arbitrary word problems, projectile motion or variable acceleration.

title: Units, volume and density
subtitle: Keep the unit attached to the number

rows: Change units when the unit is cubed
2.50 cm^3 = 0.00000250 m^3. Each centimetre contributes a factor of 1/100, so volume has a factor of 1/1000000.
Find a mass from a density and a volume
2 g/cm^3 multiplied by 3 cm^3 gives 6 g, or 0.006 kg.
See what happens when units cannot match
3 m cannot be converted to seconds without a physical relationship. A refusal is the correct result.

blocks.name: steps-answer-mathbox.png
blocks.caption: Retained emulator capture of the volume conversion. Current builds may present clearer Do, Write and Why labels inside details.

blocks.text: Density means mass per volume: mass = density * volume. The units explain why cubic centimetres cancel in the example. A bare number such as 3 does not communicate whether you mean cubic centimetres, metres or kilograms.

blocks.title: Exact scale is different from measurement precision
blocks.text: The centimetre-to-metre scale is exact. The written value 2.50 carries measured precision. StepCAS can preserve that distinction and round the displayed measurement at the end. Trailing zeros can carry information.

The native conversion family uses compatible dimensions and exact multiplicative scales. Temperature conversions requiring an offset are outside that family. The current browser runs the supplied density and conversion examples rather than exposing a general editable form.

title: Vectors, components and work
subtitle: Match directions, units and reference frames

blocks.text: A vector has components. In two dimensions, i names the horizontal basis direction and j the vertical one. A reference frame tells you what those directions mean. Adding components only makes sense when their units and frames agree.

rows: Add two movements pointing different ways
(0.00120, 0.0020) km becomes (1.20, 2.0) m. Add (5,5) m component by component. The mathematical sum is (6.20,7.0) m before final precision presentation.
Find the work done by a push at an angle
Force (2,-3) N dotted with displacement (-1,4) m gives 2*(-1)+(-3)*4 = -14 J.
Split a speed into sideways and up parts
At 10 m/s and 30 degrees above the horizontal, x = 10*cos(30 degrees) and y = 10*sin(30 degrees). The targets are 5*sqrt(3) and 5 m/s.

blocks.text: Negative work means the force component along the displacement opposes the motion. It is not a negative distance and it is not automatically an error.

items: Select a guided example and read its problem description.
Open the unit-conversion or component step first if the numbers seem surprising.
Check the stated frame and the angle unit.
Read the sign interpretation before copying the final value.

blocks.title: Where the current models stop
blocks.text: These are selected Cartesian and constant-force cases. They do not establish arbitrary rotating frames, position-dependent force work, line integrals or general three-dimensional vector lessons. A pretty vector display is not evidence that all of those operations are implemented.

title: Catch-up and relative motion
subtitle: Distinguish elapsed time from clock time

blocks.text: In the catch-up example, Atlas starts at position zero at time zero and moves at 2 m/s. Boreal starts at the same position 5 seconds later and moves at 4 m/s. Both motions use constant velocity.

Atlas:   position = 2*t
Boreal:  position = 4*(t-5), while t >= 5
Meeting: 2*t = 4*(t-5)

Solving gives t = 10 s measured from Atlas’s start. Boreal has run for 5 s. Both are at 20 m. Checking the active time interval matters. A meeting calculated before Boreal starts would not satisfy the prepared model.

blocks.name: final-relative-result.png
blocks.caption: Retained relative-motion capture. Its answer is a velocity relative to the moving reference, not a speed magnitude.

blocks.text: For relative motion, the drone’s ground velocity (36,-18) km/h is (10,-5) m/s. Subtract the wind velocity (3,1) m/s to obtain (7,-6) m/s relative to the wind. Positive horizontal and negative vertical components explain the southeast interpretation in the declared east-north axes.

blocks.title: Current access and scope
blocks.text: Both examples are available through the guided browser. They use compatible declared frames. They do not infer a coordinate transformation, solve arbitrary accelerating catch-up problems or accept a paragraph of prose as input.

title: Matrices and row operations
subtitle: Read rows as lists and follow every change

blocks.text: A matrix is a list of row lists. In the first example, the final column holds the right-hand sides of x+2*y=5 and 3*x+4*y=11. Reduced row echelon form should be [[1,0,1],[0,1,2]], so x=1 and y=2.

rows: Row echelon form. Pivots move right as you go down. Entries below each pivot are zero. Pivots need not be 1.
Reduced row echelon form. Pivots are 1 and are the only nonzero entries in their columns.
The determinant of a square matrix. The example above has determinant -2.

blocks.text: Native matrix walkthroughs record actual backend row operations and check their effect. A determinant explanation must also track how swaps and scaling affect the determinant. Row addition has a different effect from multiplying a row.

blocks.title: Current teaching envelope
blocks.text: ref and rref accept exact rational matrices with up to 4 rows and 6 columns. det accepts square matrices of orders 1 through 4. Decimal, symbolic and complex entries are outside these walkthrough families. Intermediate arithmetic can also exceed checked bounds.

blocks.title: Installed-build qualification
blocks.text: The current source includes these native command handlers, but the family catalog still marks physical keypad qualification pending. If your package lacks the required matrix backend support, record the refusal. Do not infer a successful trace from a menu entry alone.
The Matrix & Vector menu also exposes inverse, eigenvalues, decompositions and other Giac operations. Their presence does not imply native step coverage.

title: Integers and counting
subtitle: Use exact whole-number inputs for these walkthroughs

rows: 2 means proven prime in this interface.

blocks.text: A factorial multiplies the positive integers up to n. A permutation counts ordered selections. A combination counts selections where order does not matter. The distinction changes the answer even when the two input numbers are the same.

Native integer methods expect literal integer arguments. Use gcd(84,30), not gcd(7*12,30), if you want to stay inside the declared literal-input family. A mathematically equivalent compound argument can be outside that family.

blocks.title: Bounds are deliberate
blocks.text: The native family allows factorial through 100 and permutations/combinations with 0 <= k <= n <= 100. Trial-division prime and factorization lessons are bounded around one million. Division and gcd inputs are bounded around one billion. Negative inputs are supported for gcd but generally refused by the other listed methods. Resource limits still apply.

The prime-test result is a status code. Do not read 2 as “two factors.” Other probability and number commands can remain ordinary Giac operations. Device qualification for the newer integer walkthroughs remains pending in the catalog.
